stories.headline: Kalgochhia citizens travel hundreds of kilometres to support flood-hit students in Upper Assam
stories.title: Kalgochhia citizens travel hundreds of kilometres to support flood-hit students in Upper Assam
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: NAZIRA: A group of socially conscious citizens from Kalgochhia in Barpeta district extended a helping hand to students affected by the recent floods in Upper Assam by distributing educational materials at two schools in Sivasagar and Nazira.

Led by retired Chemistry professors of Navjyoti College, Kalgochhia, Abu Bakkar Siddique and Surman Ali, the team included retired principal of Chakla Higher Secondary School Ismail Hussain, Principal of Namti Piyali Phukan College Dr Dhrubajyoti Nath, college professor and Kalgochhia native Dr Shohuj Zaman, Professor Dr Putul Ngate and others.

On August 20, the team distributed school bags, notebooks, paper, pencils, pens and other educational materials among students of Rangpur Jatiya Vidya Niketan at Darikapar in Sivasagar and Nazira Uttaran Jatiya Vidyalaya at Bahgora in Nazira.

The initiative received support from former Principal of Jorhat College and noted intellectual Dr Debabrata Sharma, former headmaster and chief convenor of the Adivasi Mother Tongue Demand Committee Kiran Kumar Tanti, former general secretary of the All Assam Ravidas Samaj Rajesh Ravidas, Akash Das of Jatiya Bhawan and a large group of NSS students from Namti Swahid Piyali Phukan College.
The visiting team travelled several hundred kilometres from Kalgochhia, overcoming considerable difficulties to reach the flood-affected schools and extend support to the students.

The two schools expressed their appreciation and gratitude to the members of the Kalgochhia citizens’ group for their gesture of solidarity and compassion towards flood-affected families and students.

stories.headline: Assam: Unregulated mining threatens Kaliyani River, raises flood concerns in Numaligarh
stories.title: Assam: Unregulated mining threatens Kaliyani River, raises flood concerns in Numaligarh
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: BOKAKHAT: The Kaliyani River, along the Golaghat-Karbi Anglong border, is reportedly facing severe environmental degradation due to alleged unregulated sand and stone mining.
At Buragohain Khat, large-scale extraction is allegedly being carried out using excavators and JCB machines, raising concerns about deep excavation of the riverbed beyond authorised limits.

Although government-approved sand and gravel mahals exist along designated stretches, operators are required to comply with mining permits, environmental clearances, extraction limits and transit-challan requirements.
Environmental activist Apurba Ballabh Goswami has warned that continued destructive mining could alter the river’s course, weaken its banks and damage the aquatic ecosystem.
Concerns have also been raised about possible flooding around Numaligarh and further riverbank erosion in the Rangbong area.
The Kaliyani River is ecologically important, with the nearby Nambor-Daigrung Wildlife Sanctuary and the wider Kaziranga-Karbi Anglong landscape depending on its waterways.
Wildlife, including wild elephants, also uses the river as a source of water.
Environmental groups have called for an immediate investigation into alleged illegal or excessive mechanical mining.
Authorities have been urged to verify mining permits, environmental clearances, extraction quantities and transit challans, and to take action against any violations.

stories.headline: Iran security chief threatens neighbors against economic measures, and other Mideast developments
stories.title: Iran security chief threatens neighbors against economic measures, and other Mideast developments
stories.summary: Dubai, Aug 23: The new leader of Iran's top security body is threatening neighbours against joining new US efforts to squeeze Tehran's economy. Egypt is trying to revive Iran-US negotiations. And Iraq and Iran say Tehran has helped some ships carrying Iraqi oil to transit the Strait of Hormuz. France and Saudi Arabia are expected to discuss plans to bypass the waterway. Meanwhile, Israel has carried out strikes in Syria and in Gaza. Here's a look at the latest developments in the Iran war and the wider Middle East on Saturday. Full coverage can be found here. Iran's new top security adviser issues threats The hard-line new leader of Iran's Supreme National Security Council threatened Tehran's neighbours against joining the new US effort to hurt Iran's economy, and accused the United States of increasing global nuclear insecurity with months of war. “If (Trump) wants to do something, we will retaliate in a seismic manner,” he said in an interview with the state broadcaster that aired Saturday. Mohsen Rezaei was named this month as part of senior appointments widely seen as hardening Tehran's political and military stance. His interview with IRIB is his most extensive public statement since then. Rezaei said Iran would target oil-shipping routes out of the Persian Gulf -- alternatives to the Strait of Hormuz -- if neighbours join what he described as the economic war against Iran. Those neighbours would be considered enemies and “we will target their interests,” he said. US President Donald Trump in the past week has vowed to increase Iran's pain by imposing an “unprecedented” level of economic warfare and isolation. Iran has lived under sanctions for years. Rezaei said discussions with Oman, located on the other side of the strait, over management of it were ongoing, and said fees would be imposed. Iran asserted control over what was seen as an international waterway shortly after the US and Israel attacked on February 28. Rezaei also vowed to make changes to Iran's diplomacy and bring new capabilities to what he called the next war. He warned the US against sending more military personnel to the region, and said the US had increased nuclear insecurity because countries see that participating in international monitoring efforts, as Iran has done, is no protection against attack. Egypt tries to revive US-Iran negotiations The top diplomats for Egypt and Iran discussed efforts to bring Tehran and Washington back to the negotiating table to settle the war, Egypt's foreign ministry said. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Egyptian counterpart Badr Abdelatty also discussed the Iranian-Omani talks, the ministry said. Araghchi briefed Egypt's foreign minister about “Iran's view of ongoing developments, the course of negotiations and their challenges,” the ministry said, without elaborating. Araghchi confirmed the call. Separately, Araghchi said he had a call with Pakistan's army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir. Iran and Iraq say some Iraqi oil is facilitated through the strait The governments of Iraq and Iran said Tehran has helped some ships carrying Iraqi oil to transit the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for global oil, natural gas and other supplies, but there were few details. “There is facilitation for some ships carrying Iraqi oil in the Strait of Hormuz,” Iraqi President Nizar Amidi said in comments published Saturday by the state-run news agency, adding that Iraq doesn't have a national carrier for transporting oil. Iran's state-run IRNA news agency said a number of Iraqi oil tankers have been permitted to transit. It was not clear how many or what Iran might have received in return. Syria says an Israeli drone strike inside a village An Israeli drone strike on a vehicle wounded one person on Saturday in the southwestern Syrian village of Beit Jin, according to the Syrian state news agency SANA. Syria's foreign ministry said several civilians were injured and called the strike a flagrant violation of the country's sovereignty. The Israeli military said it targeted a “terrorist who advanced terror attacks in final stages of preparation,” without elaborating. It wasn't immediately clear if it was the same strike. Israel has carried out hundreds of airstrikes around Syria after the ouster of former President Bashar Assad in late 2024, mainly destroying army assets to keep them out of the hands of his successors. Messages differ on the Golan Heights In an interview on Friday with Mario Nawfal, a Lebanese-Australian entrepreneur, US Ambassador Tom Barrack said Israel “still” occupies the Golan Heights in violation of UN resolutions. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz on Saturday in a statement called Barrack's remarks “full of inaccuracies and positions that contradict Trump's own position.” Israel captured the Golan Heights from Syria in the 1967 war and annexed it in 1981. The UN considers the territory occupied Syrian land. But in March 2019, Trump signed a proclamation recognising Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights, reversing decades of U.S. policy. French president and Saudi crown prince will meet French President Emmanuel Macron and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman are expected to discuss plans to develop alternative routes to the Strait of Hormuz during the Saudi leader's two-day visit to Paris that starts on Sunday, according to officials in the presidency who weren't authorised to be publicly named. Proposals include increasing trade through Omani ports outside of the Persian Gulf, expanding or doubling pipelines in Saudi Arabia and elsewhere, and developing new rail links, the officials said. France and Saudi Arabia have formed a task force on energy and logistics connections between the Middle East and Europe that is scheduled to meet at the ministerial level Monday. The officials said the work would focus on identifying the most strategic projects, securing financing and establishing roles for French companies. An Israeli strike in Gaza kills 1 Palestinian An Israeli strike on the backyard of a house in central Gaza killed one Palestinian and wounded another Saturday, according to health officials at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital. Israel's military said it targeted Sharif al-Hasanat, a Hamas commander who "advanced terror attacks and took part in efforts to restore Hamas' underground infrastructure." Days earlier, a US negotiator reportedly asked Israel to draw down attacks while seeking to make progress on the ceasefire.

stories.headline: DC Sgr lays foundation stone for Addl. Accommodation Block at Zila Sainik Bhawan
stories.title: DC Sgr lays foundation stone for Addl. Accommodation Block at Zila Sainik Bhawan
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 22: Deputy Commissioner (DC) Srinagar, Akshay Labroo, who is also the President, Zila Sainik Welfare Board on Saturday laid the foundation stone for the construction of an Additional Accommodation Block at Zila Sainik Bhawan in presence of Director Sainik Welfare Department, J&K, Brigadier Pankaj Chib, SM, VSM. The proposed block is aimed at strengthening the existing infrastructure of Zila Sainik Bhawan and providing additional accommodation and welfare facilities for ex-servicemen, war widows, serving personnel and their families from across the districts of the Kashmir Division. Speaking on the occasion, the Deputy Commissioner highlighted the commitment of District Administration Srinagar towards the welfare and safe and comfortable accommodation for ex-servicemen and their dependents. He emphasized the need to ensure accessible and adequate support to members of the armed forces community through dedicated welfare infrastructure. The DC said that the additional accommodation block will enhance the accommodation capacity of Zila Sainik Bhawan and facilitate better delivery of various welfare services to eligible beneficiaries, particularly wards of ex-servicemen and martyrs who temporarily stay in Srinagar for educational purposes. He further stressed the need to incorporate a Skill Development Training Centre in the proposed block to impart skill-based training to wards of ex-servicemen and martyrs, besides local students, thereby enhancing their employability and self-reliance. On the occasion, the DC appreciated the efforts of the concerned Officers, including the Chief Planning Officer Srinagar, Superintending Engineer R&B, Executive Engineer R&B and the Zila Sainik Welfare Board, for their dedicated efforts in accelerating and completing various projects at Zila Sainik Bhawan, including the parking shed and solarisation. The DC also mentioned that 100 beded hostel for wards of ex-servicemen and martyrs has already been completed at Peerbagh and urged the Zila Sainik Welfare Board to take necessary steps for its early operationalisation so that the intended beneficiaries can avail benefit of the facility. Additional Deputy Commissioner Mir Imtiyaz Ul Aziz, Additional Deputy Commissioner Aadil Fareed, IAS Probationer Aakash Garg, Chief Planning Officer, Fayaz Ahmad Dar, Superintending Engineer, R&B North, Shabir Ahmad, Executive Engineer R&B Karan Nagar Division, Abdul Qayoom, District Social Welfare Officer, Mohammad Yousuf, Tehsildar South, Sajad Rasool Shah and senior official of Zila Sainik Bhawan including Abdul Rasid War were present on the occasion. A number of ex-servicemen, war widows, veterans and family members from various districts of the Kashmir Division also attended the event.

stories.headline: Earnings recovery still not priced in, says Kotak Life's Hemant Kanawala
stories.title: Earnings recovery still not priced in, says Kotak Life's Hemant Kanawala
stories.summary: India's earnings recovery has begun to broaden across sectors, but the market may not yet be fully pricing in the upcycle, according to Hemant Kanawala, senior executive vice president and head of equity at Kotak Life Insurance.After two weak years, relative valuations have moved closer to multi-year lows while large-caps are trading at about 19.7 times estimated FY27 earnings, Kanawala said. With Nifty profits expected to grow 17% to 18% in FY27 and Q1 earnings rising 18%, well above expectations, the setup offers a more favourable risk-reward equation, provided private capex revives and external risks remain contained.After a weak market cycle in the last 2 years, how are you assessing the current risk-reward equation in Indian equities, and what could be the key triggers for the market over the next 12 to 18 months?After two weak years, much of the bad news appears priced in. Relative valuations and performance versus emerging peers are near multi-year lows, so downside looks contained while the earnings recovery isn't yet reflected. Large-caps trade at reasonable multiples (~19.7x FY2027E), with earnings set to compound in the mid-teens.Key triggers are a durable end to the West Asia conflict and softer crude, earnings acceleration (Nifty profits +17% to 18% in FY2027), private capex revival, and a stable external position.The risks are a prolonged effect of conflict, weak monsoon, and rate tightening. Encouragingly, the Q1 profits grew 17.7% versus ~10% as expected.Are current valuations adequately reflecting the earnings growth outlook, or do you see pockets where investor expectations have run ahead of fundamentals?The market shows sharp contrasts. On aggregate it's reasonable, with the Nifty near ~19.7x FY2027E, broadly its long-term average, but this masks wide dispersion. Low-P/E sectors like banks, metals and energy anchor the index, while parts of consumption and investment trade richly, with a significant part of index weight trading over 10% above historical averages. Mid-caps and small-caps carry premiums, but this partly reflects their exposure to higher-growth themes, so selective opportunities remain attractive. Conversely, banks and IT services have de-rated meaningfully, offering value. So, earnings are priced unevenly. The froth is concentrated, not broad-based.What do you think of the current Q1 earnings cycle and which sectors surprised positively?Q1FY27 was a picture-perfect, broad-based quarter with an earnings upgrade, one of the strongest in recent years. Nifty 50 PAT grew 18% year-on-year (versus ~10% expected), a 10-quarter high, while the broader universe (ex-OMCs) delivered 22% growth. Encouragingly, many sectors beat expectations and the upgrade-to-downgrade ratio turned favourable at 1.5x. Small-caps led with 31% growth, mid-caps posted an 11-quarter-high 23%, and large-caps grew 21%. Positive surprises came from metals, Financials (BFSI), select autos and power utilities while OMCs were the key drag amid high crude.How are you positioning the portfolio amid the ongoing debate around large-caps versus mid-caps and small-caps? Have you begun seeing a meaningful shift in market leadership?We keep a balanced allocation. Large-caps offer valuation comfort, particularly banks and IT, which have de-rated. Mid-caps and small-caps trade at premiums, but that reflects their exposure to higher-growth sectors, so they remain a valuable source of alpha. Over the past three months, broader markets outperformed, with mid-cap and small-cap indices gaining mid-to-high single digits versus low single-digit returns for the Nifty, so leadership has genuinely broadened. We favour financials, hold quality compounders across the cap curve, and prefer mid and small cap selectively for an alpha kicker. A durable leadership shift ultimately needs earnings to sustain it.Which sectors currently offer the most attractive combination of earnings visibility, valuation comfort, and balance sheet strength? Conversely, which sectors appear vulnerable to an earnings downgrade?Financials screen best. Banks and insurers offer reasonable valuations, troughing margins, strong credit growth, benign credit costs, and solid balance sheets. Telecom offers earnings visibility from tariff-led ARPU gains, and discretionary consumption also provides good earnings visibility, supported by lower taxes, rate cuts and improving incomes. Metals benefit from safeguard duties and higher realisations, though it's cyclical. On the vulnerable side, we see downgrade risks in staples (margin pressure), IT services (weak discretionary demand plus AI overhang) and residential real estate (affordability strain). Energy earnings remain volatile given crude and marketing-margin swings.As a long-term equity investor managing insurance capital, how do you balance valuation discipline with the need to remain invested through market volatility? What would make you materially increase cash or reduce equity exposure?As long-term investors of insurance capital with long-dated liabilities, we stay invested through volatility rather than time the market. India's structural drivers reward patience. Importantly, we don't take cash calls in our equity funds. Discipline is expressed through allocation, favouring reasonably valued compounders and trimming froth while retaining exposure to high-growth pockets. Resilient domestic flows provide the structural support.What would make us turn materially cautious on equities: a prolonged conflict pushing crude above US$ 105 with rate tightening, a sharp deterioration in the growth-inflation mix, or fiscal slippage. Absent those, we treat corrections as opportunities to add equity from a medium-term perspective.Foreign investors have started returning after an extended phase of selling. Is this the beginning of a durable reallocation towards India or a tactical trade driven by global liquidity and currency movements?It's early to call it durable. For now it looks more tactical, though the setup for a larger reallocation is building up. Foreigners sold heavily over two years (~US$ 25bn out CYTD26), leaving positioning unusually light, with most emerging-market funds underweight India versus benchmark. Recent flows turned positive (~US$ 2bn equity in July, plus ~US$ 9bn debt), aided by currency stability and a strong Q1. Relative valuations and light positioning near multi-year lows are supportive. But a sustained reallocation likely needs global risk appetite to broaden beyond current tech-heavy markets, so India's steady growth reasserts its appeal.(Disclaimer: Recommendations, suggestions, views and opinions given by the experts are their own. These do not represent the views of The Economic Times)

Key triggers are a durable end to the West Asia conflict and softer crude, earnings acceleration (Nifty profits +17% to 18% in FY2027), private capex revival, and a stable external position.
The risks are a prolonged effect of conflict, weak monsoon, and rate tightening.
Are current valuations adequately reflecting the earnings growth outlook, or do you see pockets where investor expectations have run ahead of fundamentals?
The market shows sharp contrasts.
On aggregate it's reasonable, with the Nifty near ~19.7x FY2027E, broadly its long-term average, but this masks wide dispersion.

Low-P/E sectors like banks, metals and energy anchor the index, while parts of consumption and investment trade richly, with a significant part of index weight trading over 10% above historical averages.
Mid-caps and small-caps carry premiums, but this partly reflects their exposure to higher-growth themes, so selective opportunities remain attractive.
Conversely, banks and IT services have de-rated meaningfully, offering value.
So, earnings are priced unevenly.
The froth is concentrated, not broad-based.
What do you think of the current Q1 earnings cycle and which sectors surprised positively?
Q1FY27 was a picture-perfect, broad-based quarter with an earnings upgrade, one of the strongest in recent years.
Encouragingly, many sectors beat expectations and the upgrade-to-downgrade ratio turned favourable at 1.5x.
Small-caps led with 31% growth, mid-caps posted an 11-quarter-high 23%, and large-caps grew 21%.
Positive surprises came from metals, Financials (BFSI), select autos and power utilities while OMCs were the key drag amid high crude.
How are you positioning the portfolio amid the ongoing debate around large-caps versus mid-caps and small-caps?
Have you begun seeing a meaningful shift in market leadership?
We keep a balanced allocation.
Large-caps offer valuation comfort, particularly banks and IT, which have de-rated.
Mid-caps and small-caps trade at premiums, but that reflects their exposure to higher-growth sectors, so they remain a valuable source of alpha.

Over the past three months, broader markets outperformed, with mid-cap and small-cap indices gaining mid-to-high single digits versus low single-digit returns for the Nifty, so leadership has genuinely broadened.
We favour financials, hold quality compounders across the cap curve, and prefer mid and small cap selectively for an alpha kicker.
A durable leadership shift ultimately needs earnings to sustain it.
Which sectors currently offer the most attractive combination of earnings visibility, valuation comfort, and balance sheet strength?
Conversely, which sectors appear vulnerable to an earnings downgrade?
Financials screen best.
Banks and insurers offer reasonable valuations, troughing margins, strong credit growth, benign credit costs, and solid balance sheets.
Telecom offers earnings visibility from tariff-led ARPU gains, and discretionary consumption also provides good earnings visibility, supported by lower taxes, rate cuts and improving incomes.
Metals benefit from safeguard duties and higher realisations, though it's cyclical.
On the vulnerable side, we see downgrade risks in staples (margin pressure), IT services (weak discretionary demand plus AI overhang) and residential real estate (affordability strain).
Energy earnings remain volatile given crude and marketing-margin swings.
As a long-term equity investor managing insurance capital, how do you balance valuation discipline with the need to remain invested through market volatility?
What would make you materially increase cash or reduce equity exposure?
As long-term investors of insurance capital with long-dated liabilities, we stay invested through volatility rather than time the market.
India's structural drivers reward patience.
Importantly, we don't take cash calls in our equity funds.
Discipline is expressed through allocation, favouring reasonably valued compounders and trimming froth while retaining exposure to high-growth pockets.
Resilient domestic flows provide the structural support.
What would make us turn materially cautious on equities: a prolonged conflict pushing crude above US$ 105 with rate tightening, a sharp deterioration in the growth-inflation mix, or fiscal slippage.
Absent those, we treat corrections as opportunities to add equity from a medium-term perspective.
Foreign investors have started returning after an extended phase of selling.
Is this the beginning of a durable reallocation towards India or a tactical trade driven by global liquidity and currency movements?
It's early to call it durable.
For now it looks more tactical, though the setup for a larger reallocation is building up.
Foreigners sold heavily over two years (~US$ 25bn out CYTD26), leaving positioning unusually light, with most emerging-market funds underweight India versus benchmark.
Recent flows turned positive (~US$ 2bn equity in July, plus ~US$ 9bn debt), aided by currency stability and a strong Q1.
Relative valuations and light positioning near multi-year lows are supportive.

But a sustained reallocation likely needs global risk appetite to broaden beyond current tech-heavy markets, so India's steady growth reasserts its appeal.(Disclaimer: Recommendations, suggestions, views and opinions given by the experts are their own.
These do not represent the views of The Economic Times).

stories.headline: Imran Khan, Pakistan Army at fresh crossroads as political crisis deepens
stories.title: Imran Khan, Pakistan Army at fresh crossroads as political crisis deepens
stories.summary: The political confrontation between jailed Pakistan Tehreek- e- Insaf (PTI) founder and former prime minister Imran Khan and Pakistan’s powerful military establishment appears to have entered another critical phase, with both sides facing off over his possible release and medical treatment. According to political experts, developments being discussed in Pakistan, Army Chief and Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir has made it clear that any arrangement concerning Imran Khan, whether related to his release from prison or his transfer to a private hospital, would have to be negotiated with the military establishment rather than secured solely through an order of the Supreme Court. The issue has further widened the longstanding rift between Imran Khan and the Pakistani military. Since entering national politics, the former cricketer turned politician has repeatedly found himself at odds with successive army chiefs and senior military officers. Imran Khan’s most complicated relationship with the military establishment has involved three generals: former Army Chief General Qamar Javed Bajwa, former ISI chief Lieutenant General Faiz Hameed and current Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir. After becoming prime minister, Imran Khan appointed Faiz Hameed as Director General of the Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI). Hameed subsequently became politically close to Khan. At the time, Hameed was relatively junior in the army hierarchy but was seen as having ambitions to become army chief after Bajwa’s retirement. Bajwa was eventually given a three-year extension. Political observers at the time speculated that Hameed expected several senior officers to retire during the extension period, potentially improving his chances of becoming army chief. Relations between Imran Khan, Bajwa and Hameed, however, deteriorated. Bajwa, despite his earlier association with Hameed, ultimately backed changes in the ISI leadership. Hameed was removed as ISI chief and transferred as Corps Commander to Peshawar, while Lieutenant General Nadeem Ahmed Anjum was appointed as the new ISI chief. The relationship between Imran Khan and Asim Munir had already become strained. Munir had served as DG ISI under Bajwa in 2018 but was removed from the post after around eight months. Khan was reportedly suspicious of Munir over allegations concerning the leaking of private information relating to his wife, Bushra Bibi. The political confrontation subsequently intensified and culminated in the removal of Imran Khan’s government in April 2022 through a vote of no confidence and Shehbaz Sharif subsequently became prime minister. Munir was appointed army chief later in 2022. His rise to the top military position effectively ended Faiz Hameed’s prospects of becoming army chief. Hameed later resigned from the military and was eventually court-martialled and sentenced to 14 years in prison in a case involving allegations against him. The current confrontation comes at a time when Pakistan is facing multiple political and institutional crises. One major issue is a proposal to reorganise Pakistan’s existing four provinces into 33 administrative units. The proposal has been politically contentious, with opposition and reservations reportedly emerging within both the Pakistan Muslim League (Nawaz) and the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP). Supporters of the proposal argue that creating smaller administrative units would improve governance and ensure that development funds allocated by Islamabad reach communities at the grassroots level. However, the proposal would require broad parliamentary support and constitutional amendments. Without the backing of major political parties, including PML N, PPP and PTI, any such constitutional package would face serious difficulties in Parliament. The disagreement has also exposed tensions between the military establishment and the country’s major political parties. The military leadership is believed to be seeking political space for a possible accommodation with PTI, while the party’s principal demand remains the release of Imran Khan. This has brought the issue of Imran Khan’s imprisonment and medical treatment to the centre of the political negotiations. Imran Khan’s camp has maintained that he should either be released through judicial proceedings or shifted to a private hospital on the basis of the Supreme Court’s directions, without any political deal with the military establishment. The Supreme Court had issued directions concerning Khan’s medical treatment and access to his family. The subsequent decision to conduct his medical examination at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences in Islamabad, rather than shift him to a private facility, Shafa International Hospital has added another layer to the confrontation. The political situation has meanwhile become more complicated following the announcement of a September 27 protest and proposed long march by the PTI-led government in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. At the same time, opposition parties in the National Assembly are moving towards greater coordination over Imran Khan’s imprisonment, his medical treatment and what they describe as non-compliance with Supreme Court orders. Jamiat Ulema e Islam chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman has also begun consultations with PTI and other opposition parties on the possibility of broader political coordination. If the PPP were to join a broader opposition front, the political arithmetic in Islamabad could change dramatically. A united opposition could potentially seek a vote of no confidence against the Shehbaz Sharif government, creating a situation similar to the one that brought down Imran Khan’s government in 2022. Pakistan therefore appears to be heading towards another period of intense political uncertainty, with the military establishment, the ruling coalition, PTI and other opposition parties increasingly locked in competing strategies. The coming weeks could prove crucial for Imran Khan’s political future, the survival of the Shehbaz Sharif government and the balance of power between Pakistan’s elected institutions, the judiciary and the military establishment. Any direct confrontation between the Supreme Court and the government over compliance with judicial orders could further deepen the constitutional crisis and potentially trigger demands for a change of government or fresh elections. Pakistani political experts believe Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif and his Pakistan Muslim League Nawaz are likely to remain aligned with Army Chief and Field Marshal General Syed Asim Munir, arguing that Pakistan’s political history has repeatedly demonstrated the decisive influence of the military establishment over the country’s political system. According to political observers, Nawaz Sharif is aware of the consequences of confronting the military establishment. His political experience, particularly the events surrounding the Kargil conflict and the subsequent military takeover, remains a significant factor in determining his approach towards the army leadership. Observers believe that if the current political confrontation escalates further, Pakistan could once again face a situation in which the military assumes a more direct role in governance, a possibility that remains a major concern for the political leadership as well as the public. The stability of the Shehbaz Sharif government could also become increasingly vulnerable if the Pakistan Peoples Party withdraws its support from the ruling coalition. If the PPP pulls out of the coalition, the PML N would lose its current majority position within the government alliance and would face serious difficulty in sustaining the government without support from other parties. The National Assembly of Pakistan has 336 seats. The ruling coalition currently holds around 243 seats, while the opposition and aligned groups have 89 seats, with the remaining seats comprising independents and vacant positions. The government side includes 132 seats held by the Pakistan Muslim League Nawaz, 74 by the Pakistan Peoples Party, 22 by the Muttahida Qaumi Movement Pakistan, four by the Pakistan Muslim League Q, four by the Istehkam e Pakistan Party, one by the Pakistan Muslim League Zia, one by the Balochistan Awami Party, one by the National Party and four government-aligned independents. On the opposition side, 75 seats are held by independents and PTI-backed members. The Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam Fazl has 10 seats, while the Sunni Ittehad Council, Majlis Wahdat e Muslimeen and Pashtunkhwa Milli Awami Party have one seat each. Political analysts say the numbers underline the importance of the PPP’s support for the Shehbaz Sharif government. Any withdrawal by the PPP could dramatically alter the balance of power in the National Assembly and force the PML (N) to seek support from other political groups to remain in office. The situation has become particularly sensitive amid growing tensions between the military establishment, the ruling coalition and the opposition led by Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf. Political observers believe that the PML (N) is unlikely to risk a direct confrontation with the army leadership, given Nawaz Sharif’s previous experience of being removed from power and arrested following the military takeover under General Pervez Musharraf. With political alliances under strain and the opposition preparing for further protests, the coming weeks could determine whether the Shehbaz Sharif government survives the growing pressure or Pakistan enters another period of political instability. (The Author is a Former Bureau Chief Aaj Tak TV, Jammu)

stories.headline: Bangladesh open to joining Saudi-Pak-Turkiye defence pact: ministers
stories.title: Bangladesh open to joining Saudi-Pak-Turkiye defence pact: ministers
stories.summary: Dhaka, Aug 23: Bangladesh is open to joining the recently formed defence alliance between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye, two junior ministers have said, while stressing that any decision would be guided by the country's national interests. Signed in Makkah on August 7, the pact establishes a framework for collective deterrence and stipulates that an armed attack on any one of the three countries would be considered an attack on all three. “Bangladesh maintains a positive approach towards the possibility of joining an economic or defence framework involving Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye, taking into account its own interests and the changing dynamics of the global economy and trade,” newly appointed state minister for foreign affairs Humayun Kobir said. In an interview with the Bangla service of state-run BSS on Friday, Kobir said the government was pursuing a “Bangladesh First” policy and a balanced foreign policy with national interests at its core, which might lead Dhaka to join the defence pact. He said Bangladesh would also strengthen bilateral ties with Pakistan through normal diplomatic engagement, focusing on trade and people-to-people connectivity. Kobir, appointed as the second state minister for foreign affairs on Friday, said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is expected to visit Riyadh at Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's invitation and the tour schedule is likely to be finalised after the summer. ᨊAnother state minister for foreign affairs, Shama Obaed Islam, in a separate media interaction on Friday, supplemented Kobir’s comments, saying Bangladesh's national interest and the interests of its people would determine Dhaka’s stance on joining the pact. "Whether we join any pact or any multilateral body will be decided primarily on whether Bangladesh's interests and the interests of the Bangladeshi people are protected," she said when asked whether Bangladesh would be part of the trilateral framework. The two junior ministers' comments came two days after Rahman’s finance and planning adviser Professor Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir said a “Bangladesh First” policy marked a “paradigm shift” in the country’s foreign policy. He said the policy placed national interest, sovereignty, mutual respect and regional harmony at the centre of Bangladesh’s engagement with the international community by maintaining constructive and mutually beneficial relations with all countries. “The Bangladesh First policy means putting Bangladesh’s interests first, but Bangladesh for all,” Titumir said.

stories.headline: Heavy rain, thunderstorms lash parts of J&K; Ramban admin issues safety alert
stories.title: Heavy rain, thunderstorms lash parts of J&K; Ramban admin issues safety alert
stories.summary: Ramban , August 23 : Heavy rainfall accompanied by thunderstorms and lightning lashed several parts of Jammu and Kashmir on Sunday, prompting district administrations to issue safety advisories. In Ramban district, intense downpours and lightning were reported in different parts of the district. Taking precautionary measures, the Ramban district administration issued an alert, advising residents--especially those living in upper reaches and in close proximity to rivers, streams, and other water bodies--to remain cautious and avoid unnecessary travel during the inclement weather. Simultaneously, rain lashed several parts of the neighbouring Udhampur district, bringing down temperatures and causing wet conditions across the region. According to meteorological data, widespread precipitation and overcast conditions have led to a noticeable dip in temperatures across both Jammu and Kashmir divisions, accompanied by extremely high humidity levels. Srinagar City recorded a temperature of 16.2 degrees Celsius with 100 per cent rainfall, while Jammu City registered 22.4 degrees Celsius with 98 per cent rainfall. Among other major stations, the tourist resort of Gulmarg recorded the lowest temperature in the region at 10.6 degrees Celsius, while Pahalgam recorded 14.2 degrees Celsius alongside 96 per cent rainfall. In the Jammu division, Katra recorded 20.8 degrees Celsius with 95 percent rains, Banihal witnessed 17.4 degrees Celsius with 93 per cent showers, and Kupwara recorded 17 degrees Celsius under cloudy skies. According to the five-day forecast issued by the IMD, rainfall activity is expected to gradually taper off over the coming days, transitioning to scattered light showers across parts of southern and eastern districts including Ramban, Udhampur, Doda, Kishtwar, and Anantnag. However, the weather department has cautioned about the possibility of thunderstorms, lightning, and gusty winds reaching up to 60 km/h at isolated places, alongside the persistent risk of localised flash floods, landslides, and mudslides in vulnerable hilly terrains over the next five days. According to IMD data, across the country, very heavy rainfall was recorded over Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram, Tripura, East Uttar Pradesh, West Uttar Pradesh, and East Madhya Pradesh yesterday. Additionally, heavy rainfall was also reported over the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Assam and Meghalaya, Himachal Pradesh, West Madhya Pradesh, and Odisha. Additionally, the weather agency predicted isolated heavy rainfall for Uttarakhand from August 22 to 28. Additionally, fairly widespread rainfall is expected in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Gangetic West Bengal, Odisha, and Sub-Himalayan West Bengal and Sikkim between August 22-28, over Jharkhand from August 23-28, and over Bihar between August 24-26. (ANI)

However, the weather department has cautioned about the possibility of thunderstorms, lightning, and gusty winds reaching up to 60 km/h at isolated places, alongside the persistent risk of localised flash floods, landslides, and mudslides in vulnerable hilly terrains over the next five days.

According to IMD data, across the country, very heavy rainfall was recorded over Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram, Tripura, East Uttar Pradesh, West Uttar Pradesh, and East Madhya Pradesh yesterday.
Additionally, heavy rainfall was also reported over the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Assam and Meghalaya, Himachal Pradesh, West Madhya Pradesh, and Odisha.
Additionally, the weather agency predicted isolated heavy rainfall for Uttarakhand from August 22 to 28.

Additionally, fairly widespread rainfall is expected in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Gangetic West Bengal, Odisha, and Sub-Himalayan West Bengal and Sikkim between August 22-28, over Jharkhand from August 23-28, and over Bihar between August 24-26.

Srinagar City recorded a temperature of 16.2 degrees Celsius with 100 per cent rainfall, while Jammu City registered 22.4 degrees Celsius with 98 per cent rainfall.
